body.text: In brief
• Myanmar's security forces killed Rohingya civilians and committed violence against women and children.
• The ICJ said 10,000 were killed in Myanmar's so-called "clearance operations" to repress the Rohingya community.

Myanmar has been found responsible for genocide against its Rohingya minority in a landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), as Australia considers the implications of the decision in consultation with international partners.
The court has also ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and to be awarded compensation.
After the ruling, the country's presidential spokeswoman said the split 9-6 decision from the ICJ judges was "not fair".
"Despite efforts from our side, when we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision," Khaing Khaing Soe told reporters in Naypyidaw on Friday.
"So this was not a unanimous decision," she added. "I would say it is not fair."

The ruling by the top UN court was the first time in its 80-year history that ICJ judges have determined that a state committed genocide, and is likely to be seen as justice for Rohingya victims of Myanmar's deadly 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim minority.

"The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state," said ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa, pronouncing the verdict in the court's Great Hall of Justice in The Hague.

UN secretary-general António Guterres urged Myanmar to allow exiled Rohingya to return home. Gambian President Adama Barrow, whose country brought the case in 2019, called it a "historic day for international justice".

In Bangladesh, hundreds followed proceedings on a giant screen in Cox's Bazar — the world's biggest refugee camp housing more than one million people — with many breaking down in tears when Iwasawa pronounced the verdict.
Mohammed Osman, whose parents and four siblings were killed by the Myanmar military, said the verdict had proved that "we were not lying about the genocide".

"I am overwhelmed ... But we have achieved only 50 per cent of what we wanted. We will achieve 100 per cent when we are repatriated with dignity," Osman, 20, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.

For nearly three hours, Iwasawa laid out searing evidence of Myanmar's atrocities against Rohingyas during the campaign, which forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee into neighbouring Bangladesh.
Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed "widespread sexual violence" against women and "extreme violence" against children, Iwasawa said.
The ICJ said the evidence pointed to around 10,000 killed in Myanmar's so-called "clearance operations" to repress the Rohingya community.

Rohingya villages were "systemically destroyed" and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, said the ICJ, ruling that the "only reasonable inference" was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population which is a key test for genocide.
International reaction honours victims
Foreign Minister Penny Wong says Australia honours the victims of the genocide and pays tribute to the courage and resilience of survivors.

"Australia wants to see conditions in place that allow Rohingyas to return to their homes voluntarily, safely, sustainably and with dignity, with their human rights protected and a path to citizenship," she said in a statement, reinforcing the ICJ's court orders.
"We have taken concrete action, including imposing sanctions against members of Myanmar’s military regime and supporting international accountability mechanisms.
"The Australian Government will carefully consider the Court’s findings and their implications in consultation with our international partners.
"Australia continues to stand with the people of Myanmar."

Since 2017, Australia has committed more than $1.26 billion in humanitarian assistance to people affected by the crisis in Myanmar and Bangladesh, including Rohingya refugees and their host communities. Wong called on the Myanmar government to comply with the Court’s judgment and its obligations under international law.
Australia's Special Envoy for Indian Ocean Affairs Tim Watts said Australia regards the mass displacement of Rohungyas as a priority.

"It's a terrible humanitarian crisis, the worst in our region, and I feel enormous gratitude for Bangladesh and its people for hosting these desperate people over the last nine years," he told SBS Bangla.
"I know it's been a really significant challenge and that's why this crisis is Australia's single largest humanitarian commitment."
The UK said it would expel Myanmar's defence attache.
The US state department however reacted with caution to the ruling, saying the United States was examining the decision while stressing the need to avoid "politicisation" of the body.

The US had determined in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide but more recently it pushed back on another case before the top UN court — accusations by South Africa that Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.
"The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ," a department spokesperson said on Friday.
"We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications."
Legal experts are now looking for clues into how the court will rule in the Israel-Gaza case.
No way to enforce compliance

The case was brought by The Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to bring a case against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War Two.
The African country's justice minister told reporters at the court the verdict was a victory for the Rohingya, who had suffered great hardships.
"They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe," said Dawda Jallow.
Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.
"Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein," its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told judges during hearings in January.
While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar's rulers will adhere to the orders.

But the ruling will likely heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.
This year, he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy, which may be complicated by the ruling.
A Rohingya activist in the former capital Yangon said they were "really satisfied" by the decision, but feared potential repercussions against the community still in Myanmar.
This story was produced in collaboration with SBS Bangla and includes reporting from Sikder Ahmad.
